title: 11. The Cold War and the USA as Sole Superpower

segments.text: “Containment” is an umbrella term covering changing strategies across four decades, not one fixed method — and “sole superpower” after 1991 did not mean unlimited power, as Somalia, terrorism, Iraq and Afghanistan later demonstrated.

blocks.text: Reagan, Gorbachev, and the Unipolar Moment

segments.text: The Reagan administration expanded defence spending and adopted a more confrontational tone before later negotiating directly with Gorbachev; Soviet economic weakness and Gorbachev’s reforms accelerated the Cold War’s end, culminating in the Soviet Union’s 1991 dissolution. After 1991, the United States possessed unmatched military reach, a dominant role in global finance and alliances, and significant cultural influence — yet Somalia, terrorism, Iraq and Afghanistan later demonstrated that this dominance did not guarantee political success.

items.text: The 1970s policy of improved U.S.-Soviet and U.S.-China relations and arms control, reducing tension without ending underlying competition.
The post-1991 period of unmatched U.S. global military and economic reach, whose limits later became apparent.
Build a Cold War phase chart: containment (1947–53), nuclear confrontation, Vietnam/détente, renewed tension, ending (1985–91); for “sole superpower,” evaluate advantages and limits together.
Do not describe containment as one fixed policy used identically for forty years.
Do not say the United States “won” the Cold War through one president or one policy alone.
Do not equate sole superpower with unlimited power.
The Korean War (1950–53) internationalised containment in East Asia.
The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) brought the superpowers close to nuclear war.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, leaving the U.S. with unmatched but not unlimited global reach.
Present containment as an umbrella covering genuinely different strategies across four decades, never a single unchanging method.
“Sole superpower” status after 1991 came with real limits, later exposed in Somalia, Iraq and Afghanistan — a nuance essential to a balanced answer.
